summary: This paper develops a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a $2\times N$ silicon spin-qubit railway using coherent electron shuttling, with circuit-level noise modeling showing that the XZZX surface code outperforms CSS variants under dephasing-biased noise inherent to shuttling. A distance-7 code achieving Megaquop requires only $p = 10^{-3}$ physical error rate, reducing qubit footprint by up to 72% compared to symmetric noise models.
motivation: Silicon spin-qubit arrays face a wiring fan-out bottleneck in 2D layouts; shuttling-based 1D railway architectures offer a practical solution but require tailored error-correction strategies that account for the specific noise biases arising from micromagnet gradients and spin-orbit coupling during transport.
method: The authors derive an asymmetric Pauli-channel noise model from the underlying Hamiltonian incorporating trajectory fluctuations through micromagnet fields and spin-orbit coupling effects, implement a unidirectional 'train schedule' syndrome extraction protocol satisfying stabilizer commutation, and compare XZZX versus CSS codes under check versus data shuttling using STIM circuit-level simulations with minimum-weight perfect matching decoding.
result: Check-qubit shuttling with the XZZX code under $Z$-biased shuttling noise ($\eta = 100$, $\eta_Z = 100$) achieves a threshold of $p_\mathrm{th} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$, substantially higher than CSS alternatives; at $p = 10^{-3}$ and full bias, distance-7 XZZX requires only 97 qubits (49 data, 48 check) for Megaquop, down from 1799 qubits in symmetric noise—a 72% footprint reduction.
